object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account representing a company or entity that signs up for subscriptions. Identified uniquely by account number.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off... Six digits, sequential, never reused.
Account number, unique, never reused.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: The unique six-digit sequential identifier for an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number... Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a specific amount on a specific cycle for a specific product. Identified by subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a subscription, generated and prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offering that customers can subscribe to. Currently three exist: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: The unique code identifying a product.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: A billing artifact that specifies the price a customer pays and the billing frequency. Identified by plan code. Examples: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: The unique code identifying a price plan.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: A feature bundle representing what a customer gets: a named set of features including seat count, API access, SSO, etc. Examples: Starter, Professional, Enterprise.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: The unique name of a feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code... Is the name unique? Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a subscription becomes active.

source_references.excerpt: Start date... Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a subscription terminates. Optional for open-ended subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: End date, sometimes... An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The frequency at which a subscription is billed: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Billing period -- what are the values? Monthly or annual... Only those two... Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription indicating its current state.

source_references.excerpt: Status? Trialing, active, past due, cancelled... Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, including the effective date and who requested it. Identified by change ID.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record... It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates... It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date when a plan change becomes effective.

source_references.excerpt: when it takes effect, and those are different dates... the effective date

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person or entity who requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: Overloaded term 'plan' – three distinct concepts are called 'plan' in the system: (1) price plan (billing artifact), (2) feature bundle (feature entitlement: Starter, Professional, Enterprise), and (3) sales deal (negotiated agreement, handled separately). The model captures objects for price plan and feature bundle but does not include the sales deal concept. Clarification needed on whether the sales deal should be modeled as a separate entity type or whether it is outside the scope of this subscription model.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: The price plan... Tom: That's not what I mean by plan at all... When I say plan I mean what the customer gets... Priya: And I mean the billing artefact... Tom: We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated

ambiguities.description: Cancellation policy unclear – when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term, the system sets an end date to the paid-through date and access continues. However, the commercial policy is undecided: should cancelled customers receive a prorated refund, a credit, or no refund? This ambiguity affects whether a Refund or Credit concept should be modeled and whether a cancellation reason or refund reason should be captured.

source_references.excerpt: Someone signs an annual deal in January, pays up front, cancels in April... Priya: Nothing happens... Tom: That's not what the pricing page implies... Facilitator: So the system rule is clear, and what's unclear is whether the system rule is the business rule... Facilitator: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Paused flag overlap – a 'paused' flag exists on subscriptions but is separate from the status field (which has four values: trialing, active, past due, cancelled). Paused subscriptions appear as active in status queries due to overlapping logic. Clarification needed: is paused a true status that should be added to the four core statuses, or should it be modeled as a separate fact type (e.g., 'Subscription is paused')? Currently the model captures only the four core statuses and notes paused as outside the core model.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: There's also paused. Priya: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too... Facilitator: I'm going to record the four statuses as the status, and note that paused exists separately and overlaps confusingly.

ambiguities.description: Product count fixed or evolving – Tom states there are currently three products (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) and mentions a fourth in discovery but says he doesn't know what it is. Clarification needed: is the product list intended to be fixed at three for the purposes of this model, or should the model support arbitrary product enumeration? The model currently captures ProductCode with a constraint to the three known codes, which may need revision if new products are added.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT... Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: Plan change creation requirement – the model captures that a subscription has a 'current plan' field and that plan changes provide the history. However, it is unclear whether the current plan field is mandatory at creation (i.e., every subscription must start with a plan change) or whether the initial plan is set directly on the subscription record without creating a plan change entry. Clarification needed on whether the first plan is represented as a PlanChange or stored differently.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record... the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history... And a brand new subscription has none [plan changes]... Right, none until something changes.

ambiguities.description: MRR derivation inputs – Sam confirms that MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) is derived from price plan and billing period, but the model does not include a 'Price' or 'Amount' value type attached to PricePlan. Clarification needed: what fact type stores the price amount on a PricePlan? Is it a simple field, or does pricing vary by Account or other dimensions? The model currently excludes MRR as a stored attribute (correctly) but does not explicitly model the price data from which it is computed.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR... It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month... I called it a field because that's how I see it in my dashboards, but nothing writes it.

ambiguities.description: Account identifier reuse policy – Priya states that account numbers are never reused: if an account closes and the same company returns, they get a new number and are treated as a new customer. However, Tom notes this is problematic from a product perspective because the company's history is lost. Clarification needed: should the model support a historical relationship linking old Account numbers to the same company (e.g., a Company entity with multiple Accounts)? The current model treats each Account as independent and does not track company history.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused. If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer... Tom: Which drives me mad... because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: Billing period constraint completeness – Priya confirms that a subscription has exactly one billing period (monthly or annual) and that both cannot apply to a single subscription. However, the model does not capture whether certain feature bundles or products might only support certain billing periods (e.g., premium features available only on annual billing). Clarification needed: is billing period chosen independently by the customer for any price plan, or are there constraints linking BillingPeriod to PricePlan or FeatureBundle?

source_references.excerpt: Can a subscription be both? No... You cannot bill someone monthly and annually for the same subscription, that's just billing them twice... Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

ambiguities.description: Feature bundle pricing – the model captures that every PricePlan entitles exactly one FeatureBundle, but it is not clear whether a FeatureBundle may have multiple price points (e.g., different monthly vs annual prices, or prices varying by region/customer). Currently the model implies a FeatureBundle is independent of pricing, but the fact type 'PricePlan entitles FeatureBundle' does not capture pricing details. Clarification needed on whether FeatureBundle pricing is many-to-one (multiple PricePlans per Bundle at different prices) or whether other pricing dimensions exist.

source_references.excerpt: Every price plan gives you exactly one feature bundle. CORE-MO-49 and CORE-AN-490 both give you Professional... There's a monthly and an annual for each bundle, and sometimes a legacy one we haven't retired.
